prize_parts.citation: for developing empirical methods to estimate demand, market power and competition in differentiated-product industries

statement.case_for: My preferred part is unchanged: a single achievement, B012, credited to Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn. The criteria I apply are originality, durable use and exact credit. Random-coefficients demand with endogenous prices (Berry 1994; Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes 1995) gave economists a way to recover substitution patterns, markups and welfare from market data. That is discovery through measurement, and not only technique. It changed what regulators and researchers can credibly conclude in merger review, antitrust, trade, health and environmental work. From a corporate-finance background, what I value most is theory built to be tested on real data and then adopted in practice. The record here is about thirty years of replication, software, and identification and computational critique, and the method has stayed standard through all of it. That is the strongest evidence of maturity I can point to. I have narrowed the citation from round 1. It now names demand, market power and competition in differentiated-product industries, and it no longer names dynamic industry models. Berry and Levinsohn are not credited with the dynamic strand. A narrower wording also answers the worry that the award would claim all of empirical IO. Pakes's dynamic-games work remains a reason to place him in the trio, but the citation does not depend on it. Reassessing after the exchange, I did not find a decisive argument that moves another candidate above B012. The comparison with B002 is a real difference in judgment about mechanism versus measurement, and I do not think the record settles it.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains attribution. Seven names are credited and a three-person cap leaves out Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin. If Bresnahan's earlier work on market power and product differentiation were judged equal in kind to the BLP breakthrough, no three-person set around BLP would be fully defensible. This is a real weakness, and I rely on my own recollection of how credit divides because I cannot verify it here. Second, the prize would reward a toolkit, and some members place conceptual mechanisms above measurement. Third, structural identification rests on functional-form and equilibrium assumptions, and those critiques are still active. Fourth, my round 1 text said the field has no earlier laureate. I withdraw that as an argument for merit. Field novelty is not merit, and I cannot verify the claim from the supplied evidence. Finally, B002 is the cleaner two-author origin and has the broadest opening reach. I do not count that reach as scientific merit, but its clean credit is a real advantage on attribution.

responses.point: Teorell proposes a two-part configuration: Kiyotaki and Moore for B002, and Pakes alone for B012. He treats Pakes as the anchor of the estimation programme, records the omission of Berry and Levinsohn as a real attribution loss, and accepts that the pairing has no obvious shared theme.
responses.response: I take the proposal seriously, because it respects the three-person cap. I would not prefer it to a B012 trio. The central demand-estimation breakthrough is the BLP paper, and Pakes alone credits the programme while leaving out the two co-authors of its best-known result. A prize should not buy room for a second part with an exact-credit cost, and Teorell himself says the cost is real. The thematic gap between collateral-driven credit cycles and empirical IO is also real. A combined citation would be a bundle of two separate achievements chosen to fit a cap, not a single connected insight. I would rather present B012 as a single, exactly credited part. I agree with his reading of the common-criteria test, though, and I regard B002 for Kiyotaki and Moore as the cleanest component of his configuration.

responses.point: The chair says my argument and those of Andersson and Hjalmarsson moved him to add B012 as an alternative. He keeps B002 first because he finds the mechanism's originality and its effect on macro modelling and policy greater. He separates Gertler's later intermediary-based quantitative work from the 2022 recognition and keeps him as a third name.
responses.response: I appreciate that, and I agree the choice between B002 and B012 is a judgment about weighting, not an error by either side. On Gertler I disagree with the three-name version. The intermediary-based work with Kiyotaki and Karadi concerns bank balance sheets and financial intermediation. That is closer to the ground of the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises than the collateral mechanism is, so it strengthens the overlap objection. It does not weaken it. His credit is also divided between B002 and the eight-name B043, and a clearly bounded citation is a virtue. If the Committee chose B002, I would support Kiyotaki and Moore alone. That is a change from my opening proposal, which included Gertler. On the chair's mechanism-versus-method question, my criterion is what the contribution established and how well it has survived testing in use. A mechanism whose quantitative size is still debated has a thinner empirical record than a method that has remained the working standard for three decades. I hold that view lightly.

responses.point: Krusell reports that he narrowed B002 to Kiyotaki and Moore. He attributes to me the claims that Gertler is the natural remaining name given Bernanke's 2022 prize, and that Gertler's credit is split with B043. He disagrees with the first claim and accepts the second.
responses.response: I want to correct the record. My round 1 text did not make either argument. My opening ballot did include Gertler in the B002 proposal, but I did not write a case for him, and the B043 point was made by others. I agree with Krusell's conclusion. The accelerator lineage has other originators, one of them already a laureate, and adding Gertler would leave Gilchrist as an obvious omission and blur the credit. I no longer support a three-name B002. I also share his hesitation about letting wide use stand in for a discovery. My answer is that BLP is both a method and a set of findings about markups, substitution and merger effects, but I accept that others may weigh the two differently.

responses.point: Andersson agrees that BLP with Pakes as anchor is the cleanest attribution. He keeps Bresnahan out of the preferred part because his contribution is earlier and more separable. He says field novelty should not count as merit, and that he cannot verify that no earlier prize touched empirical IO.
responses.response: I accept his correction and I have dropped field novelty from my case. The case rests on reach, durability and attribution clarity. I agree that Bresnahan is separable from the specific demand-estimation breakthrough. Hjalmarsson's counterpoint is the honest limit of that view. If Bresnahan's contribution were judged equal in kind, the set would need rethinking. I cannot resolve that from the supplied evidence, and I would want the Committee to test it directly. Benkard and Levin raise a separate point. Their work belongs to the dynamic-game strand, which is why I narrowed the citation to demand, market power and competition. A demand-focused citation understates Pakes's dynamic work, and I accept that cost.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B025 first and B012 third. He sees Melitz as changing what economists think the mechanism of trade gains is, whereas BLP is mainly a toolkit for estimating demand. He would not oppose B012 if the Committee prefers methods used across fields.
responses.response: I take the mechanism-versus-method distinction seriously, and it is the main substantive disagreement between us. I would answer that BLP changed what is known as well as what can be estimated. It supplied credible estimates of substitution, markups and welfare effects that altered merger and regulatory conclusions in actual industries. On B025, I agree the Melitz mechanism is distinct from Krugman's 2008 prize, and that the exporter-premia and selection evidence is strong. My remaining reservation is the credited set. The exporter facts and parts of the theory came from Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not on the ballot, and Pareto-based results are sensitive to functional form. A Melitz-Helpman citation would have to be worded carefully. B025 is still my second alternative, behind B002 on attribution cleanliness alone.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson agrees on the compactness of the BLP core. She worries that if Bresnahan's contribution were judged equal in kind, no three-person set around BLP would be fully defensible. She would word the citation narrowly so it does not imply credit for all of empirical IO.
responses.response: I share both points and have acted on the second by narrowing the citation. The Bresnahan question is the single issue most likely to change my own view of B012. If members who know the empirical IO literature better than I do judged his contribution to be of the same kind and weight as BLP, I would move B012 down and treat B002 for Kiyotaki and Moore as my fallback. On the supplied evidence, I read his work as foundational to the field but separable from the specific demand-estimation inversion. That is a judgment from my own recollection, not verified credit analysis.

uncertainties: Whether Bresnahan's contributions on market power and product differentiation are equal in kind to the BLP breakthrough. If they are, no three-person B012 set is fully defensible. I rely on recollection and have not verified the credit split.

Whether the Committee weighs conceptual mechanisms and measurement frameworks equally, which is the main reason I rank B012 above B002. This is a real difference in judgment, and I cannot settle it from the record.

How strongly the evidence supports quantitatively large collateral-driven amplification (B002), compared with how well structural demand estimation has withstood identification and computational critique.

How much weight to give adjacency to the 2008, 2022 and 2024 prizes. My view is that overlap is a balance and timing question and not a demerit of the discovery, but it is a judgment, and the files do not settle it.
Whether the credited sets for B025 (Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum) and B012 (Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard, Levin) can be defended against omitted contributors.
I have not independently verified citation counts, publication dates, relative credit within the structural-IO group, or whether any earlier prize touched this area.
statement.conflict_note: Updated from round 1. The profile lists no co-authorship with any credited name on B012, B002 or B025. Its co-authors (Kaplan, Axelson, Weisbach, Jenkinson, Lerner, Sørensen, Robinson, Martinsson, Thomann) are not candidates. My field is corporate finance. B002 (collateral constraints and credit cycles) is adjacent to financial contracting, and B012 and B025 are not adjacent, so my round 1 statement that no shortlisted candidate is adjacent should be corrected for B002. I discount any affinity for it. The profile records long committee overlap with Hassler and Krusell, who prefer B002, and with Ellingsen and Svensson. These are colleague relationships, not candidate-specific connections. I am Vice President of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences and served on the Swedish Financial Crisis Committee in 2011 to 2013. Neither bears on a credited name. Disclosed without adjudication.
